name: Low-glycemic diet (for acne)
lead: A low-glycemic diet (low-GI or low-glycemic-load diet) is an eating pattern built around carbohydrates that raise blood glucose slowly, such as legumes, whole grains and most vegetables, in place of white bread, sugary drinks and sweets. People use it to get clearer skin: the idea is that steadier glucose and insulin levels lead to fewer breakouts and less oily skin, without drugs.[1][4]

The glycemic index, introduced by David Jenkins and colleagues in 1981, ranks carbohydrate foods from 0 to 100 against pure glucose, and glycemic load adjusts that ranking for portion size.[2] Wikipedia's acne article reports that randomized and non-randomized studies have found lower-glycemic-load diets reduced acne, and that dermatologists commonly suggest a diet low in simple sugars; it also describes the diet-and-acne evidence as emerging.[1]

Several small randomized trials have measured lesion counts, hormones and skin biopsies on low-glycemic-load diets in people with acne, with reductions in lesion counts reported in 10 to 12 week studies.[4][5][6] Glycemic index itself has recognized limitations: values depend on ripeness, cooking and processing, and individual responses differ.[2]

chain: Lower glucose and insulin swings, lower IGF-1 in trials
angle.text: People adopt a low-glycemic diet to reduce acne lesions and oiliness so their skin looks clearer. In trials, participants eating low-glycemic-load diets showed lower lesion counts and, in one study, smaller sebaceous glands on biopsy.

paras: The glycemic index rates carbohydrate-containing foods by their effect on blood glucose over two hours relative to a reference such as glucose; foods scoring 55 or less are classed as low, 56 to 69 as medium and 70 or more as high.[2] Glycemic load multiplies GI by the grams of carbohydrate in a serving and divides by 100.[2]

A low-glycemic diet for acne emphasizes low-GI carbohydrates and reduces refined, high-GI items. No single standard version exists; trial diets have ranged from low-GI carbohydrate with higher protein to plain low-GL advice.[4][5]

Proponents and some clinicians propose that high-glycemic meals produce larger insulin responses, which are thought to raise IGF-1 and androgen activity, increasing sebum production and follicular blockage.[1] Wikipedia notes that androgens and IGF-1 both appear to be essential for acne, since acne does not develop in complete androgen insensitivity syndrome or in Laron syndrome, which involves low IGF-1.[1]

A 2007 randomized trial in 43 males aged 15 to 25 compared a diet of about 25% protein and 45% low-GI carbohydrate with a carbohydrate-dense control diet for 12 weeks. Lesion counts fell more in the low-glycemic-load group, which also lost more weight and improved insulin sensitivity; the authors noted that weight loss may have contributed.[4] A second 2007 randomized, investigator-masked trial of 43 male patients with a high-protein, low-glycemic-load diet reported greater lesion reduction, a lower free androgen index and higher IGFBP-1, again with weight loss as a possible contributor.[5]

A 2012 Korean randomized trial in 32 patients with mild to moderate acne ran 10 weeks. The low-glycemic-load group had fewer inflammatory and non-inflammatory lesions, and biopsies showed smaller sebaceous glands, less inflammation and lower SREBP-1 and IL-8 expression.[6] A 2018 randomized trial in 66 adults with moderate to severe acne found that IGF-1 fell significantly after two weeks on a low GI/GL diet, while glucose, insulin and body composition did not differ; the authors called for longer studies.[7]

Many larger low-GI trials have studied diabetes and weight rather than skin, for example a meta-analysis of low-GI diets in diabetes management.[3] The acne trials are small and short, and the field is described as emerging.[1]

Wikipedia lists several caveats: GI values change with ripeness and cooking, individual responses vary from day to day, GI ignores portion size and insulin response, and some low-GI foods such as chocolate cake and ice cream are not otherwise considered healthy.[2] A 2023 Cochrane review, cited there, found low-GI or low-GL diets did not produce more weight loss in overweight adults than other approaches.[2]

timeline.event: David Jenkins and colleagues introduce the glycemic index.[2]
Two randomized trials of low-glycemic-load diets in young men with acne are published.[4][5]
Korean randomized trial reports lower lesion counts and smaller sebaceous glands on a low-glycemic-load diet.[6]
Two-week randomized trial reports lower IGF-1 in adults with moderate to severe acne.[7]

card.summary: Eating low-GI carbs to calm acne: the one diet tweak with some trial support, though the evidence is modest.
card.note: Glycemic index values vary with ripeness, cooking and the individual, and diet is not a substitute for medical acne care.

quick.overview:
A low-glycemic diet swaps fast-digesting carbohydrates such as white bread, sugary drinks and sweets for slower ones such as legumes, whole grains and most vegetables. In looksmaxxing and skincare circles it is discussed as a way to reduce acne without drugs.

According to Wikipedia's acne article, several randomized and non-randomized studies have reported that lower-glycemic-load diets reduced acne severity, and dermatologists commonly suggest a diet low in simple sugars. The overall body of evidence is described as emerging rather than settled.
quick.mechanism: The proposed mechanism is that high-glycemic meals raise blood glucose and insulin, which is thought to increase IGF-1 and androgen activity, and in turn sebum production and comedone formation. Androgens and IGF-1 are both considered important in acne biology.
quick.risks: A low-GI eating pattern is generally an ordinary dietary approach with no specific safety concerns identified in the sources. Glycemic index is an imperfect measure: some foods with a low GI are high in fat or sugar, and values vary between individuals and preparations.
